Contributors run, build, and test the ADK locally with new feature, enhancement. After that, they can connect to a production instance of watsonx orchestrate.

Practices.Summary: In April 2026, IBM developers shipped the Build-Time Evaluation Experience — a simulation engine that lets builders run hundreds of synthetic conversations against an agent from within the UI before any real user sees it. Builders record a real conversation, let the system auto-extract key details into structured test cases, then re-run those test cases on demand to get a Journey Success score. Every time an agent's instructions or tool descriptions change, the builder re-runs the suite and watches the score move — replacing hours of manual spot-checking with a repeatable automated benchmark.

evidence.quote: This powerful new experience enables you to simulate hundreds of conversations at once, giving you fast, comprehensive insights into how your agent behaves in the real-world scenarios.
Build-time agent testing: Validate your agent's behavior during the build phase, catching issues before they impact users.
Automated test case generation: Key details are automatically extracted from saved conversations and converted into structured test cases, minimizing manual effort.
re-run your tests to quickly see how your agent's success rate improves over time, no more hours spent on manual testing.

Practices.Summary: Kelly To shipped the Debug Experience in April 2026, giving builders an interactive visual canvas to step through agent execution turn-by-turn during development. Rather than hunting through raw JSON logs or OpenTelemetry spans, the developer can navigate a structured execution timeline and inspect the input, reasoning, and output at each individual step. When the agent routes incorrectly, the builder reviews the reasoning logic, adjusts agent instructions or tool descriptions, and reruns — a tight loop that catches behavioral drift before release.

evidence.quote: As agents become more powerful, the real challenge is no longer building them — it's understanding them.
Builders can now understand how the agent arrives at its answer and why it behaves the way it does, through an intuitive, visual representation of agent execution.
Digestible trace data: Translate complex trace logs into a clear, visual format, no more digging through raw JSON or OTEL logs.
Navigate Through the Execution Timeline: Move through the execution step-by-step, observing the input, reasoning, and output of each step.
Make targeted fixes after understanding where and why the agent deviated from expected behavior.

Practices.Summary: The ADK ships a built-in red-teaming command group that simulates 15+ adversarial attack types against an agent — prompt injection, instruction override, role-play bypass, social engineering, encoded-text inputs, and foreign-language exploits — aligned to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM09 Misinformation). Builders run a subset of attacks first to validate their setup, then expand with the `-n` flag for broader variant coverage. The resulting attack success rates become a measurable benchmark developers improve against before deploying to production.

evidence.quote: The LLM agent vulnerability testing is designed to test the robustness and security of AI agents by simulating adversarial scenarios. It helps identify vulnerabilities in agent behavior, such as susceptibility to prompt injection, instruction override, or social engineering attacks.
Red-teaming is a security practice where a group (the 'red team') simulates real-world attacks to identify weaknesses in a system before malicious actors can exploit them.
Start with a small set of attacks to validate your setup. Use -n to limit variants for faster iterations. Review success rates to identify weak points in your agent's defenses.

Practices.Summary: Agent behavior is evaluated against a formal ground-truth schema before deployment. Each test scenario is a structured JSON dataset containing the agent name, a dependency graph of expected tool calls, the desired tool arguments for each call, the expected final response quality, a human-readable 'story' of the user intent, and an opening sentence. The evaluation engine compares the agent's actual 'trajectory' (its live tool-call sequence and generated response) against this schema using a multi-tier fuzzy-match pipeline — LLM-as-judge first, then cosine similarity, then fuzzywuzzy WRatio — so natural-language variations in parameter values do not fail valid trajectories.

evidence.quote: The evaluation framework in the ADK is designed to assess agent behavior by comparing simulated agent interactions, referred to as trajectories, against a predefined set of reference data.

A trajectory is considered successful when: The agent performs all required tool calls in the correct order with the expected input parameters. The agent generates a high-quality summary that effectively addresses the user's query.
Agent evaluation is driven by a user story, which provides all necessary context for the agent to perform tool-based tasks.

Tools.Summary: The ADK's internal test suite is managed by the Hatch build system by executing the full pytest suite and generating a coverage report. The Build-Time Evaluation Experience, agent Debug Experience, and red-teaming CLI are all first-party testing tools embedded in the ADK.

Practices.Summary: The Developer Edition — the local production replica that developers test against — ships as a Docker Compose application managed entirely through the `orchestrate server` CLI. On startup, the server initializes infrastructure containers (PostgreSQL, MinIO, Milvus), runs Liquibase database migrations automatically, and waits until all services are healthy before accepting connections. The ADK 2.0.0 release was a major breaking change: it removed the separate Docker engine dependency (Rancher Desktop, Colima) that users previously had to install separately, requiring existing users to run `orchestrate server reset` followed by `docker system prune -a --volumes` before upgrading.

Issues.issue_title: Fixed mismatch with UI around OpenAPI specs with mutliple servers
Issues.issue_description: The ADK CLI disagreed with the Builder UI on how to handle OpenAPI specifications that declared multiple server entries, causing import or runtime failures when users had multi-server API definitions.

Issues.issue_title: Fix remote toolkits using host.docker.internal
Issues.issue_description: Remote Python toolkits running inside Docker containers could not resolve the host machine address via the host.docker.internal hostname, breaking tool connectivity in Developer Edition environments.

Issues.issue_title: Fix flow export with MCP tool Nodes
Issues.issue_description: Flows containing MCP tool nodes failed to export correctly; the exported JSON was missing or corrupting MCP node data, preventing flow portability across environments.

Issues.issue_title: Fix context passing in python tools when using futures package
Issues.issue_description: Python tool functions that used the `futures` concurrency package could not read or update the agent's shared context object, silently dropping context modifications during concurrent tool execution.

Issues.issue_title: Fix team OAuth credentials configured from the ADK
Issues.issue_description: OAuth credential objects configured through the ADK CLI were not correctly applying team-level scope, causing authentication failures when multiple team members attempted to share the same credential.

Issues.issue_title: Increase timeout of agent deployment command to 5 minuts and add env var WXO_AGENT_DEPLOYMENT_TIMEOUT to control it
Issues.issue_description: The `orchestrate deploy` command was timing out on slow networks or large agent configurations before the deployment confirmed success, leaving builders unable to determine if their deploy had worked.

Issues.issue_title: Fix for CPD environment activation with irregular urls
Issues.issue_description: Cloud Pak for Data (CPD) environment activation via the ADK CLI failed when the CPD cluster URL contained non-standard path segments or trailing slashes, blocking enterprise on-premises users from connecting.

Issues.issue_title: Fix text wrapping in AI builder dry-run output
Issues.issue_description: The `--dry-run` output from the AI builder subcommand was wrapping text incorrectly, making the printed plan difficult to read in standard terminal widths.

Issues.issue_title: Tools with bytes return type can now modify context
Issues.issue_description: Python tool functions with a `bytes` return type annotation were silently prevented from writing to the agent context object, a regression introduced in a prior release that blocked file-handling tools from persisting state.

Issues.issue_title: AI builder autotune not converting guideline tools from id to name
Issues.issue_description: During AI builder autotune, tool references stored as internal IDs were not being converted to their human-readable names before being written into the agent's configuration, causing downstream routing failures.

Issues.issue_title: Auto-discover command unhidden
Issues.issue_description: The `orchestrate tools auto-discover` command was accidentally hidden from the CLI help output after a refactoring pass, making it undiscoverable to new users even though the command was fully functional.

Issues.issue_title: AI builder not working if agent had non-native collaborators
Issues.issue_description: Agents that listed non-native (external) collaborator agents in their configuration caused the AI builder to fail entirely, preventing any AI-assisted configuration on multi-agent orchestration setups.

Issues.issue_title: Python tools that export bytes are not able to update context (Known Issue, 2.3.0)
Issues.issue_description: A known limitation documented in the 2.3.0 release: tool functions returning byte payloads could not also modify the agent's context map. The team flagged this transparently in the Known Issues section before resolving it in 2.4.0.

Issues.issue_title: In developer edition chat with docs is working in preview chat but not in the main chat (Known Issue, 2.3.0)
Issues.issue_description: Chat-with-documents functionality worked in the Preview Chat panel but not in the primary chat interface in the Developer Edition, creating a confusing inconsistency for builders testing knowledge-base-enabled agents.

Issues.issue_title: Pre-filled Parameters in flow tool
Issues.issue_description: Parameter values that were pre-filled in flow tool node configurations were being dropped or ignored at runtime, requiring users to re-enter values the flow was supposed to supply automatically.

Issues.issue_title: Fixed docstrings not parsing input descriptions
Issues.issue_description: Python tool functions whose docstrings used certain formatting styles had their parameter description text silently discarded, causing tool parameter descriptions to appear blank in the Agent Builder UI.

Issues.issue_title: Fixed timestamp bug when exporting knowledge bases
Issues.issue_description: Timestamps on knowledge base export manifests were incorrectly formatted or out of sync, causing re-import failures when builders moved knowledge bases between environments.

Issues.issue_title: Bugfix: deleting an agent no longer deletes its knowledge base
Issues.issue_description: Deleting an agent was inadvertently cascading to delete the agent's associated knowledge base, destroying data the builder intended to keep and reuse with a replacement agent.

Issues.issue_title: [Bug] 'Build with AI' feature not functional, Agent Builder UI in Orchestrate - IBM Cloud (Using Techzone environment)
Issues.issue_description: Community-reported (Tony Begemy, March 2026): the 'Build with AI' feature in the Agent Builder UI was non-functional in IBM Cloud Techzone environments, blocking builders from using the AI-assisted agent configuration workflow.

Issues.issue_title: HTTP 415 at Orchestrate Developer Edition server start
Issues.issue_description: Community-reported (Moab Alves Silva, April 2026): the Developer Edition server start sequence returned HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type errors during initialization, preventing the local development environment from starting.

Issues.issue_title: High latency in agents responses
Issues.issue_description: Community-reported (Ramya Swarna, April 2026): builders observed consistently elevated response latency from watsonx Orchestrate agents under normal load, prompting discussion of timeout configurations and model selection strategies.

Practices.Summary: The ADK documentation formalizes a four-stage iterative development lifecycle that every builder follows before deploying an agent to production: (1) Develop — build and configure the agent using the ADK CLI and Python tools; (2) Evaluate — run the trajectory evaluation suite against a ground-truth dataset to measure Journey Success; (3) Analyze — inspect failing trajectories to identify whether bugs lie in tool definitions, agent instructions, or parameter routing; (4) Improve — update the relevant artifact, re-run evaluations, and watch the score change. This loop is designed to repeat as many times as needed within the Developer Edition before production deployment ever occurs.

evidence.quote: The agent development process before deployment is iterative and consists of four key stages: Develop, Evaluate, Analyze, Improve.

Use your evaluation results as a benchmark. As you adjust agent instructions, update tool descriptions, or modify the tools themselves, re-run your tests to quickly see how your agent's success rate improves over time.

Practices.Summary: The ADK team ships on a bi-weekly minor-release train with semantic versioning (2.0.0 through 2.9.0 across six months, averaging one release every two weeks). Each release consolidates contributions from multiple product squads — ADK, Developer Edition, Flows, Evaluations, Channels, Observability, Builder, AI Gateway — into a single tagged version. Breaking changes are called out in a dedicated section with explicit migration steps, and the team maintains backwards compatibility within major versions. This cadence forces continuous integration discipline: squads must merge and stabilize contributions within each two-week window.
